prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made incretin-based therapy of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: Round 1 left one real question on the table, which is the principle for the third name. I hold that this prize should reward a discovery of how the body works that made a medicine possible. B007 is the clearest example on the shortlist: proglucagon processing, the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36) and the receptor biology led to a drug class with replicated outcome-trial benefit in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease. Nobody disputes its maturity, and recognition now carries almost no risk of reversal. Under that principle, Drucker and Holst are fixed, and the third name should be someone credited with identifying and making the active peptide. On the supplied record that is Mojsov. I keep Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, with a citation that names the physiology and the active form and says nothing of any product.
statement.case_against: The case against my configuration is serious, and round 1 did not remove it. First, Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is disputed in the literature, and Habener is not on the supplied list, so a citation that names her may read as a ruling on a priority question I cannot verify from this record. I have tried to word the citation so that it credits the discovery of the active form without saying who found it first. Second, omitting Knudsen leaves out the person whose acylation work turned a peptide with a half-life of minutes into a once-daily and once-weekly drug, and a prize without her can look like it separates the science from the medicine. The three-person cap makes this a forced choice, and I do not think that choice is costless. Third, the committee may be crediting a contested trio for the basic science while the commercial product is what the public sees.

responses.point: Sandberg and the chair argue that the acylation-based half-life extension is what turned GLP-1 physiology into a medicine, so Knudsen should be the third name, and Sandberg says he would accept the Mojsov trio if the committee wants a purely discovery-level prize.
responses.response: That concession is the part of your argument that moves me most, and I think the committee should take it up directly, because it says the whole disagreement is about principle. I accept that the physiology alone did not produce a usable drug, and I do not call Knudsen's work routine engineering. But the physiology and the active peptide are what made it possible to ask the question, and her work is a development of that finding. My difficulty with your configuration is the cost of the principle, which is that it would honour a company's central achievement in a prize meant for discovery. I would move if the committee agrees that this prize should explicitly name drug design. On a discovery-level reading I stay with Mojsov, and I note that you would accept that outcome.

responses.point: The chair argues that including Mojsov rests on a priority claim that no one has verified, and says he would move if the committee judges peptide identification to be more decisive than acylation-based development.
responses.response: Your objection is fair: I cannot verify Mojsov's priority from the supplied record and I said so in round 1. But the same gap applies in the other direction. If we leave her out because the claim is uncertain, we settle an open question against her without evidence, and that is a decision, not a neutral act. My answer is to give the third name to the contribution the citation describes, identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) form, and to word it so the citation does not say who was first. That treats the dispute honestly. I also agree with you that Holst and Drucker are the scientific anchors, so we differ only on one name. If you are asking whether I would shift on principle, my answer is that peptide identification does outweigh acylation for a prize meant to reward discovery.

responses.point: Linnarsson holds Mojsov as the third name but says he would move only if the record showed her priority to be weaker than credited, and keeps B041 with June and Sadelain as the strongest alternative, with Rosenberg outside.
responses.response: I am in the same position on Mojsov: I would reverse only on evidence about priority, and the supplied record has none either way, so I do not think the dispute is a ground to drop her. On B041 we still differ over Rosenberg. I think his adoptive cell transfer and early gene-modified T-cell trials are foundational, so a pair without him is a real judgement and not a neutral one, and Eshhar's absence from the list makes me more cautious than you about B041 as the first part of a prize. For this round that does not matter, since I keep it as my first alternative, as you do, and not as a second part.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks B004 (Walter and Mori) above B041 as the first alternative, citing cleaner attribution and mechanism, and holds Mojsov as the third B007 name.
responses.response: I agree that B004 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and that its mechanism has stood for about three decades. I still place B041 first, because durable remissions in patients are a consequence that B004 cannot yet match, and I regard that as a difference in clinical reach and not in scientific quality. Both stay as my alternatives. I also repeat that Ron and Kaufman are not in the supplied credit, so the clean two-name attribution depends on how the list was drawn up. If B007 stalls on credit and the committee wants a different winner, B004 would be an easier choice on names and B041 on clinical impact, and I would not think either choice was wrong.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to identifying and synthesising the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide should be credited when her priority relative to Habener and others cannot be verified from the supplied record.
Whether the committee wants the prize to reward discovery, which supports Mojsov, or drug development, which supports Knudsen, since a three-person cap forces the choice.
Whether the citation can be worded to credit the active form without ruling on who was first, and without reading as a prize for a commercial product.
Whether the originators of the chimeric-receptor concept, such as Eshhar, who is not credited in B041, would change my view of June, Sadelain and Rosenberg as a fallback.
Whether a two-part prize pairing B007 with B004 or B041 can fit within three people. I think it cannot, since B007 needs three names, so I treat the prize as a single B007 part.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. My profile records a group-leader affiliation at the Broegelmann Research Laboratory in Bergen and past co-authors Vijay Kuchroo and Sven-Erik Sonesson. None of them is credited on any shortlisted ballot, and I infer no personal tie from shared institutions or topics. I need no recusal.
